title: Governing AI across borders: risks, institutions and the UK’s role
label: 16 September 2026 · Multilateralism and AI
summary: Witnesses Sam Daws (University of Oxford) and Isabella Wilkinson (Chatham House) told the Lords committee that AI raises a wide range of shared, cross-border risks—safety failures, security threats, misuse, information harms and environmental impacts—and that current international responses are a fragmented patchwork of UN processes, regional rules, standards bodies and minilateral groups. They argued for practical steps: better testing and incident reporting, standards and evaluator networks, closer private-sector engagement with accountability, stronger UK diplomatic coordination, and targeted capacity building for the global south. A new global agency is possible but unlikely without a major incident; the short-term priority is to strengthen existing institutions and interoperability.

chapters.title: What multilateral AI governance needs to address
chapters.takeaway: AI governance must cover safety, security, regulatory consistency, trust in information, inclusion, public-health opportunities and environmental effects.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’ll focus on how multilateral institutions can manage AI. Sam, what are the key governance issues they need to address?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Main issues are safety—agreeing how to evaluate advanced AI and share risk info; international security, from cyberattacks to militarised AI and AI-enabled biological threats; and regulatory interoperability between the EU, US, China and others.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Also important are cultural and linguistic inclusion so AI reflects global needs; information integrity to limit AI-driven interference in elections; science and public health benefits; and environmental impacts from data centres.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I group governance problems into three linked types: shared risks (malicious misuse, loss of control, systemic risks like discrimination), lack of trusted information about AI impacts, and weak preparedness—no established crisis toolbox for AI-driven disruptions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. That frames the scale: public safety, security, standards, trust and preparedness.

chapters.title: The current international picture: patchwork and pockets of progress
chapters.takeaway: Global AI governance is a nascent, fragmented mix of UN dialogues, regional laws, standards bodies and minilaterals; there are some promising technical best practices but little binding global law.

turns.speaker: Lord Ahmad of Wimbledon
turns.text: There are many organisations—UN, G7, OECD, Council of Europe. Is there space for one model to prevail?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Right now it’s a global patchwork stuck in intense gridlock. There’s lots of discussion—UN dialogues and summits—but few binding outcomes and little 'connective tissue' to implementation.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Some successes exist at the technical level: better incident reporting, model transparency norms pushed by the G7 and OECD, and the UN’s recent scientific panel work. Those small technical agreements can scale if we learn from them.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There are three levels: universal (UN resolutions and scientific panels), regional (EU’s law-heavy approach; other regions focus on data, language and local needs), and minilateral groups like the G7, Bletchley follow-ups and other coalitions. Private sector forums also matter.

turns.speaker: Lord Lamont of Lerwick
turns.text: Will we see convergence in small groups rather than a single global agreement?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Yes—expect convergence in smaller groupings and persistent global fragmentation. The goal should be better interoperability between those threads so harms don't slip through gaps.

chapters.title: Hard technical and political problems
chapters.takeaway: Three core barriers are the dual-use nature of AI and geopolitics, companies’ commercial secrecy, and the technology’s opacity—made harder by new agentic behaviour.

turns.speaker: Baroness Crawley
turns.text: Where are the hardest challenges—top-layer uses, technical layers, or human-rights questions?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Three big, cross-cutting problems: geopolitical competition and AI’s dual-use nature; companies’ reluctance to reveal model internals for commercial reasons; and the technology itself—models are opaque and move fast.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Agentic AI complicates things: models acting in the world can collude, deceive or behave unpredictably. Governance must cover pre-release testing and post-release life-cycle monitoring.

turns.speaker: Baroness Crawley
turns.text: So we need testing, reporting and ways to control systems after deployment?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Exactly—testing helps but isn’t a silver bullet. We need independent evaluation, post-deployment monitoring, thresholds for intervention and the capacity to act when models cause harm.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: But if a company says it was safe when released and harm comes from how users deploy it, who’s accountable?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: That’s an attribution problem. We need clarity across supply chains: who modified a model, who deployed it and where. Agent identification, tracking and staged permissioning are part of the technical fixes.

chapters.title: Private companies and standards: partnership with accountability
chapters.takeaway: The private sector is central—frontier capabilities are mostly private—so governments must work with companies but insist on accountability, shared testing and clearer responsibilities.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: Should private companies have a formal role in global governance, and how do we make sure action follows agreement?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Companies already shape governance—technical norms often start inside firms. Governments must accept that and bring companies in, but with reciprocity and enforcement: independent evaluators, access for testing and clear accountability.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: There’s debate inside industry—some leaders back third-party evaluators; others oppose tighter rules. The UK can help incubate independent evaluator networks and trusted technical standards.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Historically Western minilaterals and voluntary forums drove practice. We need to widen that to include Chinese firms and others so standards are interoperable globally, not just within western coalitions.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blackstone
turns.text: Do we need a new global body to govern AI?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Avoid reinventing the wheel—strengthen and resource existing networks (technical forums, the UN dialogue, standards bodies). Create permanent secretariats or better mandates for what already works rather than a wholly new organisation today.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: A dedicated global agency is conceivable but unlikely without a major crisis that convinces states to cede power. Short term: push standards, evaluator networks, and better interoperability across existing bodies.

chapters.title: What the UK can and should do
chapters.takeaway: The UK has technical expertise and diplomatic reach; it should coordinate government, back evaluator networks, lead capacity-building for other countries, strengthen standards work, and engage the private sector and China pragmatically.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prashar
turns.text: Does the UK have what it takes to shape multilateral AI talks, and how should government make best use of it?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Yes. The UK’s strengths are technical expertise (AI Security Institute), diplomatic heritage (Bletchley summit minilateralism) and partnerships, especially with the US and Commonwealth. But Whitehall must be better joined-up and act quickly.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: The UK can combine science diplomacy and practical capacity building: help countries adopt safe, locally relevant AI, back UN agencies that work at national level, and offer expertise rather than just aid cheques.

turns.speaker: Lord Bruce of Bennachie
turns.text: So we should redeploy diplomatic effort overseas to help emerging economies adopt AI safely and reap productivity gains?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Yes—use scenario-based training and capacity-building for governments facing AI-driven disruption, and push standards work that helps countries test and secure models and supply chains.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Practically, that means the UK should align with allies on regulation where useful, maintain access to US frontier models for testing, engage China where possible, and tailor offers by region—Central Asia, Africa, Latin America all need different support.

turns.speaker: Lord De Mauley
turns.text: How does China’s WAICO differ from western-led bodies and what does that mean for allies?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: China stresses sovereignty, diffusion, and full-stack support for local contexts. It offers low-cost, interoperable approaches that appeal to many countries; the West needs comparable offers and to seek interoperability, not just confrontation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final practical recommendations for this committee to pass to government?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Two priorities: back an independent evaluator ecosystem (UK technical authority) and use UK diplomatic convening—via the G20 and other fora—to build minimum multilateral consensus on priority issues like biosecurity and standards.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Echo that: focus on AI safety, security and AI for science; ensure joined-up UK engagement with US, EU and China where possible; and offer targeted capacity building to the global south using the UK’s technical and diplomatic assets.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. That concludes our session—very helpful and practical evidence for our report.
